```{r setup}
slope <- function(x, y) sum((x - mean(x)) * (y - mean(y))) / sum((x - mean(x))^2)
dm    <- function(z, g) z - ave(z, g)
nickell <- function(a, m) {                            # Nickell (1981) plim of FE bias, m = T-1 AR obs
  if (m < 3) return(-(1 + a) / 2)
  A <- 1 - (1 / m) * (1 - a^m) / (1 - a)
  B <- 1 - (2 * a / ((1 - a) * (m - 1))) * (1 - (1 - a^m) / (m * (1 - a)))
  -((1 + a) / (m - 1)) * A / B
}
gen_panel <- function(N, T, rho, su = 1, se = 1, on_target = TRUE) {   # T x N matrix of levels
  u <- rnorm(N, 0, su)                                 # on_target: start at own long-run level
  y <- (if (on_target) u / (1 - rho) else 0) + rnorm(N, 0, se / sqrt(1 - rho^2))
  M <- matrix(0, T, N); M[1, ] <- y
  for (t in 2:T) M[t, ] <- rho * M[t - 1, ] + u + rnorm(N, 0, se)
  M
}
f2 <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f", x)
```

## Where we left off

- The panel lecture rested on one claim: anything about a firm that **does not change** cannot explain why its outcome changed. Demean, and the firm effect is gone.
- The price was **strict exogeneity**: today's shock must not feed into tomorrow's regressors.

\vspace{0.4em}

- Finance is full of outcomes that depend on **their own past**: leverage, payout, cash, investment.
- Put yesterday's $Y$ on the right-hand side and strict exogeneity is not merely doubtful. **It is false by construction.**
- This lecture: what breaks, how badly, how to fix it --- and when the fix does not work.

## The plan

1. **Why the past belongs on the right-hand side** --- and one rule that settles every calculation.
2. **Two estimators, two wrong answers.** They err in opposite directions, which turns out to be useful.
3. **The fix: instruments from the past.** Anderson--Hsiao, then Arellano--Bond.
4. **Why the fix can fail** --- and system GMM, which fails differently.
5. **In practice:** a case study from capital structure, the code, and a checklist.

\vspace{0.4em}

- Two running questions. *Which comparison is this estimator making?* And, new this week: *which way is it wrong?*

# 1. Why the Past Belongs on the Right-Hand Side

## Most things in finance drift

They do not jump to a target. They close part of the gap each year.

\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabular}{ll}
\toprule
Leverage & firms close only part of the gap to target each year \\
Payout & managers smooth dividends, and cut only as a last resort \\
Cash & drawn down quickly, rebuilt slowly \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

$$
Y_{it} \;=\; \rho\,Y_{i,t-1} + \delta D_{it} + u_i + \varepsilon_{it}, \qquad |\rho| < 1
$$

- $\rho$ **is the economics.** $1-\rho$ is the share of the gap closed per year; a shock has half-life $\ln(0.5)/\ln\rho$. At $\rho = 0.6$ that is $1.4$ years; at $\rho = 0.9$, $6.6$ years. **Different theories of the firm.**
- $\delta$ is now the **impact** effect. The long-run effect is $\delta/(1-\rho)$ --- get $\rho$ wrong and you get *that* wrong too.

## What a firm effect does to a series

```{r two-firms}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 2.0
#| out-width: 78%
#| fig-align: center
set.seed(3); rho <- 0.6; T <- 25
one <- function(u) { y <- u / (1 - rho) + rnorm(1, 0, 1 / sqrt(1 - rho^2))
  out <- numeric(T); for (t in 1:T) { y <- rho * y + u + rnorm(1); out[t] <- y }; out }
yA <- one(1); yB <- one(-1)
par(mar = c(2.6, 2.8, 0.3, 0.3), mgp = c(1.6, 0.5, 0), cex = 0.9)
plot(1:T, yA, type = "l", lwd = 2, ylim = range(c(yA, yB)), xlab = "year", ylab = expression(Y[it]), las = 1)
lines(1:T, yB, lwd = 2, lty = 2)
abline(h = c(1, -1) / (1 - rho), col = "grey60", lty = 3)
text(T, 1 / (1 - rho) + 0.6, expression(u[i] == +1), adj = 1, cex = 0.9)
text(T, -1 / (1 - rho) - 0.6, expression(u[i] == -1), adj = 1, cex = 0.9)
```

Two firms, same $\rho = 0.6$, same shocks in distribution --- different $u_i$. Back-substitute the model into itself:
$$
Y_{it} \;=\; \frac{u_i}{1-\rho} \;+\; \delta\sum_{j\ge0}\rho^{\,j}D_{i,t-j} \;+\; \sum_{j\ge0}\rho^{\,j}\varepsilon_{i,t-j}
$$

- The firm effect shifts the **level** --- not the volatility, not the persistence. Each firm wiggles around its own long-run level $u_i/(1-\rho)$.
- **Remember this picture.** An estimator that cannot tell *high because it was high last year* from *high because this firm is simply high* will get $\rho$ wrong.

## One rule settles every calculation

$Y_{is}$ is assembled from $u_i$ and from shocks **dated $s$ and earlier** --- nothing later. If $\varepsilon_{it}$ is serially uncorrelated and unrelated to $u_i$:
$$
\boxed{\;\mathbb{E}[Y_{is}\,\varepsilon_{it}] = 0 \;\;\text{whenever}\;\; t > s,
\qquad
\mathbb{E}[Y_{is}\,\varepsilon_{is}] = \sigma^2_\varepsilon\;}
$$

- In words: **a later shock has nothing to do with an earlier $Y$**; the same-date shock enters $Y$ with coefficient one.
- Every derivation in this lecture is a **date check**: write out a product, compare the two dates, and it is either zero or $\sigma^2_\varepsilon$.
- One clause does quiet work: *serially uncorrelated*. It turns out to be the identifying assumption of the whole enterprise --- and it is testable.

## The problem you cannot assume away

Lag the model one period and the difficulty is on the page:
$$
Y_{i,t-1} \;=\; \rho\,Y_{i,t-2} + \delta D_{i,t-1} + \underbrace{u_i}_{\text{\textbf{also in today's error}}} + \;\varepsilon_{i,t-1}
$$

- Every endogenous regressor so far was endogenous because of something we **failed to measure**. This one is endogenous **by construction**.
- $Y_{i,t-1}$ contains $u_i$, and so does the error: **pooled OLS is biased.**
- $\varepsilon_{it}$ moves $Y_{it}$, which *is* next year's regressor: strict exogeneity is false, so **fixed effects is biased too.**
- The useful part: **they fail in opposite directions.**

# 2. Two Estimators, Two Wrong Answers

## Why OLS reads heterogeneity as persistence

```{r rho0}
set.seed(4242)
.T <- 5; .N <- 100000                                  # rho = 0 exactly; sigma_u = sigma_e = 1
.M  <- matrix(rep(rnorm(.N), each = .T), .T, .N) + matrix(rnorm(.T * .N), .T, .N)
.id <- rep(1:.N, each = .T - 1)
.yc <- as.vector(.M[2:.T, ]); .yl <- as.vector(.M[1:(.T - 1), ])
z0 <- c(ols = slope(.yl, .yc), fe = slope(dm(.yl, .id), dm(.yc, .id)))
```

Strip the model to the bone. Set $\rho = 0$ --- **no persistence whatsoever**, only permanent differences between firms:
$$
Y_{it} \;=\; u_i + \varepsilon_{it}
$$

- A high-$u_i$ firm is high this year **and** was high last year --- not because the past caused the present, but because the firm is simply like that.
- Pooled OLS sees $Y$ following $Y$ and calls it persistence:
$$
\operatorname{plim} \hat\rho_{\text{OLS}} \;=\; \frac{\operatorname{Cov}(Y_{it}, Y_{i,t-1})}{\operatorname{Var}(Y_{i,t-1})} \;=\; \frac{\sigma^2_u}{\sigma^2_u + \sigma^2_\varepsilon} \;>\; 0 \;=\; \rho
$$
- With $\sigma_u = \sigma_\varepsilon = 1$ that is $0.5$. Simulated ($T=5$, $100{,}000$ firms): $\hat\rho_{\text{OLS}} = \mathbf{`r sprintf("%.3f", z0["ols"])`}$ when the truth is **zero**.
- **More years do not help.** More years of the same firm being itself is more of the same evidence.

## Why demeaning manufactures mean reversion

**The story.** A lucky year raises $Y_{i,t-1}$ **and** the firm's average. Measured against that inflated average, the firm's other years look low --- so the firm *seems* to revert even when nothing reverts.

\vspace{0.3em}

In symbols: the firm mean contains the errors, so after demeaning
$$
\underbrace{Y_{i,t-1} - \bar Y_{i,-1}}_{\text{regressor}}
\quad\text{is correlated with}\quad
\underbrace{\varepsilon_{it} - \bar\varepsilon_{i}}_{\text{error}}:
\qquad
\operatorname{Cov}\big(Y_{i,t-1},\, -\bar\varepsilon_i\big) \;<\; 0, \;\; \text{of order } \sigma^2_\varepsilon/T
$$

- So $\hat\rho_{\text{FE}}$ is biased **down**: **Nickell (1981) bias.**
- The same $\rho = 0$ experiment with fixed effects: $\hat\rho_{\text{FE}} = \mathbf{`r sprintf("%.3f", z0["fe"])`}$, almost exactly $-1/(T-1)$. OLS invented persistence; demeaning invents **mean reversion**.
- It happens **even if $u_i$ does not exist** --- demeaning alone does it --- and it fades only at rate $1/T$.

## A derivation you can do at the board: $T = 3$

With $T = 3$ there is **one differenced observation per firm**, and $\hat\rho_{\text{FE}}$ is exactly least squares on $\Delta Y_{i3} = \rho\,\Delta Y_{i2} + \Delta\varepsilon_{i3}$:
$$
\operatorname{plim}(\hat\rho_{\text{FE}} - \rho) \;=\; \frac{\mathbb{E}[\Delta Y_{i2}\,\Delta\varepsilon_{i3}]}{\mathbb{E}[(\Delta Y_{i2})^2]}
$$

- **Numerator, by the rule.** Expand $(Y_{i2} - Y_{i1})(\varepsilon_{i3} - \varepsilon_{i2})$ into four products. Three pair a $Y$ with a *later* shock: zero. One pairs $Y_{i2}$ with its *own* shock, with a minus sign: $-\sigma^2_\varepsilon$.
- **Denominator, from the picture.** $u_i$ cancels in a difference; what is left has variance $2\sigma^2_\varepsilon/(1+\rho)$.
$$
\operatorname{plim}(\hat\rho_{\text{FE}} - \rho) \;=\; \frac{-\sigma^2_\varepsilon}{2\sigma^2_\varepsilon/(1+\rho)} \;=\; -\,\frac{1+\rho}{2}
$$
- **The plim of $\hat\rho_{\text{FE}}$ is negative for every $\rho<1$**: leverage that is genuinely $90\%$ persistent is reported as mean-reverting. (Hansen 2022, §17.37.)
- Keep that $-\sigma^2_\varepsilon$ in mind. It comes back in Section 3.

## Watching both biases at once

Simulate $Y_{it} = \rho Y_{i,t-1} + u_i + \varepsilon_{it}$ with $\rho = 0.6$ and $4{,}000$ firms, varying the number of years $T$.

```{r bias-table}
#| results: asis
set.seed(20260202)
rho <- 0.6; N <- 4000
est <- function(T) {
  M <- gen_panel(N, T, rho)
  id <- rep(1:N, each = T - 1)
  yc <- as.vector(M[2:T, , drop = FALSE]); yl <- as.vector(M[1:(T - 1), , drop = FALSE])
  c(slope(yl, yc), slope(dm(yl, id), dm(yc, id)))
}
Ts <- c(3, 5, 10, 30)
r  <- sapply(Ts, est)
brk <- r[, 2]                                           # T = 5: OLS, FE
np <- rho + sapply(Ts - 1, function(m) nickell(rho, m))
cat(sprintf(
"\\begin{center}\\small
\\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
\\toprule
Years per firm & $T=3$ & $T=5$ & $T=10$ & $T=30$ \\\\
\\midrule
Pooled OLS \\quad(biased \\textbf{up}) & $%.3f$ & $%.3f$ & $%.3f$ & $%.3f$ \\\\
Fixed effects \\quad(biased \\textbf{down}) & $%.3f$ & $%.3f$ & $%.3f$ & $%.3f$ \\\\
\\quad \\emph{Nickell (1981) plim, for comparison} & \\itshape %.3f & \\itshape %.3f & \\itshape %.3f & \\itshape %.3f \\\\
\\midrule
Truth & $0.600$ & $0.600$ & $0.600$ & $0.600$ \\\\
\\bottomrule
\\end{tabular}
\\end{center}
", r[1,1], r[1,2], r[1,3], r[1,4], r[2,1], r[2,2], r[2,3], r[2,4], np[1], np[2], np[3], np[4]))
```

- **The OLS row never moves.** Heterogeneity is not resolved by more years.
- **At $T = 3$ fixed effects is negative** for a process with persistence $+0.6$ --- as $-(1+\rho)/2$ predicted.
- The FE row tracks Nickell's plim throughout: this is bias, not noise.

## Does it fade with $T$? Slowly.

```{r nickell-plot}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 2.6
#| out-width: 85%
#| fig-align: center
Tgrid <- 3:50
par(mar = c(2.6, 3.2, 0.3, 0.3), mgp = c(1.7, 0.5, 0), cex = 0.9)
plot(NA, xlim = c(3, 50), ylim = c(-1, 0), xlab = "years per firm, T", ylab = "plim of FE bias in rho", las = 1)
abline(h = 0, col = "grey60"); abline(v = c(10, 20), col = "grey80", lty = 3)
for (k in 1:3) {
  a <- c(0.3, 0.6, 0.9)[k]
  lines(Tgrid, sapply(Tgrid - 1, function(m) nickell(a, m)), lwd = 2, lty = k)
}
legend("bottomright", bty = "n", lwd = 2, lty = 1:3, cex = 0.95,
       legend = c(expression(rho == 0.3), expression(rho == 0.6), expression(rho == 0.9)))
```

- The bias is $O(1/T)$: doubling the panel halves it. Finance panels are typically $10$--$20$ years, often unbalanced.
- At $T = 30$ the bias is still $`r sprintf("%.3f", nickell(0.6, 29))`$ at $\rho = 0.6$ and $`r sprintf("%.3f", nickell(0.9, 29))`$ at $\rho = 0.9$. **The more persistent the series, the slower the bias leaves.**

## Two wrongs that bound the right answer

Neither estimator is consistent. But you know the **sign of each bias**, so together they fence the truth in:
$$
\hat\rho_{\text{FE}} \;<\; \rho \;<\; \hat\rho_{\text{OLS}}
$$

- In the table at $T=5$: $`r f2(brk[2])` < 0.60 < `r f2(brk[1])`$. Wide, and **honest**. A single number from either estimator would not be.
- **The standard first move** (Bond 2002): run OLS and fixed effects *before* anything clever, and keep both numbers. They are the goalposts.
- **Any estimator you trust must land between them.** One that lands outside tells you something is wrong before you interpret a single coefficient.
- A bracket is a statement about **bias**, not a confidence interval.

\vspace{0.2em}
\footnotesize
(A second bracket, for $\delta$ when you are unsure whether the lagged-$Y$ or the fixed-effects model is right, is in the backup.)
\normalsize

# 3. The Fix: Instruments from the Past

## The fix, in one idea: Anderson--Hsiao

Difference the model to kill $u_i$:
$$
\Delta Y_{it} \;=\; \rho\,\Delta Y_{i,t-1} + \delta\,\Delta D_{it} + \Delta\varepsilon_{it}
$$

- But $\Delta Y_{i,t-1}$ contains $\varepsilon_{i,t-1}$, and so does $\Delta\varepsilon_{it}$: the same $-\sigma^2_\varepsilon$ as the $T=3$ derivation. **Differencing is not the fix; it is where the fixed-effects bias comes from.**
- **So go back one more lag.** $Y_{i,t-2}$ is **far enough back to be clean**, yet **close enough to still predict** $\Delta Y_{i,t-1}$.
- That is **Anderson--Hsiao (1982)**: IV on the differenced equation, instrumenting $\Delta Y_{i,t-1}$ with $Y_{i,t-2}$. It needs $T \ge 3$.
- The lagged outcome caused the problem, and a *longer* lag of the same variable solves it --- no new data, only the history you already have.

## One date apart: a broken regressor and a valid instrument

Check each piece against the rule, with $\Delta\varepsilon_{it} = \varepsilon_{it} - \varepsilon_{i,t-1}$:

\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabular}{lccc}
\toprule
 & $\times\,\varepsilon_{it}$ & $\times\,\varepsilon_{i,t-1}$ & $\mathbb{E}[\,\cdot\,\Delta\varepsilon_{it}]$ \\
\midrule
$Y_{i,t-1}$ & $0$ (later shock) & $\boldsymbol{\sigma^2_\varepsilon}$ \textbf{(same date)} & $-\sigma^2_\varepsilon$ \\
$Y_{i,t-2}$ & $0$ (later shock) & $0$ (later shock) & $0$ \\
\midrule
$\Delta Y_{i,t-1} = Y_{i,t-1} - Y_{i,t-2}$ & & & $\boldsymbol{-\sigma^2_\varepsilon}$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

- **Validity.** The regressor inherits the one same-date term; the instrument, one year older, has none. **The difference between a broken regressor and a valid instrument is one date.**
- **Relevance.** $u_i$ cancels inside $\Delta Y_{i,t-1}$, leaving $\operatorname{Cov}(Y_{i,t-2},\Delta Y_{i,t-1}) = -\sigma^2_\varepsilon/(1+\rho) \neq 0$. Nonzero --- but Section 4 shows it can still be weak.
- **The zero row rests on the quiet clause.** If $\varepsilon$ is serially correlated (fit AR(1) when the truth is AR(2)), $\varepsilon_{i,t-2}$ inside $Y_{i,t-2}$ predicts $\varepsilon_{i,t-1}$ and the instrument is invalid. **Lag length is the identifying assumption** --- tested two slides on.

## Arellano--Bond: use every lag you have

Anderson--Hsiao uses one moment condition out of many. At date $t$, **every** $Y$ dated $t-2$ or earlier passes the date check (Holtz-Eakin, Newey and Rosen 1988; Arellano and Bond 1991):

\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabular}{lll}
\toprule
Differenced equation at & valid instruments for $\Delta Y_{i,t-1}$ & how many \\
\midrule
$t = 3$ & $Y_{i1}$ & 1 \\
$t = 4$ & $Y_{i1},\, Y_{i2}$ & 2 \\
$t = 5$ & $Y_{i1},\, Y_{i2},\, Y_{i3}$ & 3 \\
$\;\;\vdots$ & & \\
$t = T$ & $Y_{i1},\, \dots,\, Y_{i,T-2}$ & $T-2$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

- A **block-diagonal** instrument matrix with $(T-1)(T-2)/2$ columns; overidentified once $T > 3$, so the estimator is **GMM**.
- **Gain:** efficiency --- one-instrument Anderson--Hsiao is very noisy. **Cost:** the count grows with $T^2$: $91$ instruments at $T = 15$, $406$ at $T = 30$.

## Too many instruments

Roodman (2009): GMM with many instruments relative to $N$ is quietly a bad estimator.

- **It overfits.** With enough instruments the first stage reproduces $\Delta Y_{i,t-1}$ almost exactly, contaminated part included, and GMM slides back toward **OLS on its own equation**. For difference GMM that is OLS on the differences --- biased **down**, below even fixed effects. (For system GMM, Section 4, it is pooled OLS: biased **up**.)
- **It disarms the overidentification test.** Hansen's $J$ becomes too weak to reject anything; a $p$-value of $0.99$ is a warning sign, not a clean bill of health.
- **Two standard remedies.** *Cap the lag depth* (say $Y_{i,t-2}$ to $Y_{i,t-4}$). *Collapse*: one column per lag, so the count grows with $T$, not $T^2$.
- Keep the count **well below $N$**, and **report it**.

## Two-step weights, and the tests you must report

- **One step or two.** Two-step GMM re-weights with first-step residuals: efficient, but its standard errors are **badly biased down** in finite samples. Use the **Windmeijer (2005)** correction (`twostep vce(robust)` in Stata). If one-step robust and two-step Windmeijer disagree, something is weak.
- **AR(1) in the differenced residuals --- expected.** $\Delta\varepsilon_{it}$ and $\Delta\varepsilon_{i,t-1}$ share $\varepsilon_{i,t-1}$.
- **AR(2) --- must be absent.** $\Delta\varepsilon_{it}$ and $\Delta\varepsilon_{i,t-2}$ share nothing *unless $\varepsilon$ is serially correlated*. This is the test of the quiet clause; fail it and **every instrument is invalid**.
- **Hansen $J$**, with the instrument count beside it.
- **The bracket.** Difference GMM near or below $\hat\rho_{\text{FE}}$: weak or too many instruments --- they pull the same way. Anything above $\hat\rho_{\text{OLS}}$: a violated assumption (Section 4 shows one).

# 4. Why the Fix Can Fail

## Weak instruments: the first stage, in closed form

Blundell and Bond (1998) wrote the first stage, $\Delta Y_{i,t-1} = \gamma\,Y_{i,t-2} + v_{it}$, and divided covariance by variance:
$$
\begin{aligned}
\gamma \;&=\; \frac{\operatorname{Cov}(Y_{i,t-2},\Delta Y_{i,t-1})}{\operatorname{Var}(Y_{i,t-2})}
\;=\; \frac{-\sigma^2_\varepsilon/(1+\rho)}{\sigma^2_u/(1-\rho)^2 + \sigma^2_\varepsilon/(1-\rho^2)} \\[0.3em]
&=\; (\rho - 1)\,\frac{k}{k + \sigma^2_u/\sigma^2_\varepsilon},
\qquad k = \frac{1-\rho}{1+\rho}
\end{aligned}
$$

\vspace{-0.4em}

- The covariance on top never vanishes; **the damage is all in the denominator.** The *level* $Y_{i,t-2}$ is swamped by things that say nothing about the *change*.
- **As $\rho \to 1$**, a random walk's level says nothing about its next step.
- **As $\sigma^2_u/\sigma^2_\varepsilon$ grows**, the level is mostly the firm's permanent height, which cancels out of the change. In the two-firm picture: the heights tell you nothing about the wiggles.
- Both are the normal case in corporate finance: **persistent series, large firm effects.**

## A picture of the first stage

```{r gamma-plot}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 2.6
#| out-width: 85%
#| fig-align: center
gam <- function(rho, r) { k <- (1 - rho) / (1 + rho); (rho - 1) * k / (k + r) }
rg <- seq(0, 0.99, by = 0.01)
par(mar = c(2.6, 3.2, 0.3, 0.3), mgp = c(1.7, 0.5, 0), cex = 0.9)
plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(-1, 0), xlab = expression(rho), ylab = "first-stage coefficient", las = 1)
abline(h = 0, col = "grey60")
for (k in 1:3) { vr <- c(0.25, 1, 4)[k]; lines(rg, gam(rg, vr), lwd = 2, lty = k) }
legend("bottomright", bty = "n", lwd = 2, lty = 1:3, cex = 0.95,
       legend = c(expression(sigma[u]^2/sigma[epsilon]^2 == 0.25), expression(sigma[u]^2/sigma[epsilon]^2 == 1), expression(sigma[u]^2/sigma[epsilon]^2 == 4)))
```

- At $\rho = 0.6$ with equal variances, $\gamma = `r sprintf("%.2f", gam(0.6, 1))`$: a usable first stage. At $\rho = 0.95$, $\gamma = `r sprintf("%.4f", gam(0.95, 1))`$ --- essentially nothing.
- Leverage, payout and cash all sit in the right-hand third of this plot. **The instrument is weakest exactly where you most need it.**

## Watching it fail

Same design: $500$ firms, $T = 6$, $200$ replications. **Median** and **10th--90th percentile** across replications.

```{r four-est}
#| results: asis
estimators <- function(M) {
  T <- nrow(M); N <- ncol(M)
  id <- rep(1:N, each = T - 1)
  yc <- as.vector(M[2:T, ]); yl <- as.vector(M[1:(T - 1), ])
  ols <- slope(yl, yc); fe <- slope(dm(yl, id), dm(yc, id))
  dY  <- M[3:T, , drop = FALSE] - M[2:(T - 1), , drop = FALSE]      # Anderson-Hsiao
  dY1 <- M[2:(T - 1), , drop = FALSE] - M[1:(T - 2), , drop = FALSE]
  Z2  <- M[1:(T - 2), , drop = FALSE]
  ah  <- sum(Z2 * dY) / sum(Z2 * dY1)
  m <- T - 2; L <- m * (m + 1) / 2                                  # one-step GMM
  H <- diag(2, m); H[abs(row(H) - col(H)) == 1] <- -1               # difference block
  Hs <- rbind(cbind(H, matrix(0, m, m)), cbind(matrix(0, m, m), diag(m)))   # + levels block
  ZHZ <- matrix(0, L, L); ZX <- numeric(L); ZY <- numeric(L)
  SZ <- matrix(0, L + m, L + m); SX <- numeric(L + m); SY <- numeric(L + m)
  for (i in 1:N) {
    Zi <- matrix(0, m, L); c0 <- 0                                  # Arellano-Bond: Y_1..Y_{t-2}
    for (s in 1:m) { Zi[s, c0 + 1:s] <- M[1:s, i]; c0 <- c0 + s }
    ZHZ <- ZHZ + crossprod(Zi, H %*% Zi)
    ZX  <- ZX + crossprod(Zi, dY1[, i]); ZY <- ZY + crossprod(Zi, dY[, i])
    Zs <- rbind(cbind(Zi, matrix(0, m, m)),                         # system: + levels eq.,
                cbind(matrix(0, m, L), diag(dY1[, i], m)))          #   instrument dY_{t-1}
    Xs <- c(dY1[, i], M[2:(T - 1), i]); Ys <- c(dY[, i], M[3:T, i])
    SZ <- SZ + crossprod(Zs, Hs %*% Zs); SX <- SX + crossprod(Zs, Xs); SY <- SY + crossprod(Zs, Ys)
  }
  W  <- solve(ZHZ); ab  <- as.numeric((t(ZX) %*% W  %*% ZY) / (t(ZX) %*% W  %*% ZX))
  Ws <- solve(SZ);  sys <- as.numeric((t(SX) %*% Ws %*% SY) / (t(SX) %*% Ws %*% SX))
  c(ols = ols, fe = fe, ah = ah, ab = ab, sys = sys)
}
set.seed(1)
sims <- list(a = replicate(200, estimators(gen_panel(500, 6, 0.6))),
             b = replicate(200, estimators(gen_panel(500, 6, 0.95))),
             c = replicate(200, estimators(gen_panel(500, 6, 0.95, on_target = FALSE))))
med  <- lapply(sims, function(s) apply(s, 1, median))
cell <- function(s) apply(s, 1, function(v)
  sprintf("$%.2f$ \\;{\\footnotesize[$%.2f$, $%.2f$]}", median(v), quantile(v, .1), quantile(v, .9)))
s6 <- cell(sims$a); s95 <- cell(sims$b)
cat(sprintf(
"\\begin{center}\\small
\\begin{tabular}{lcc}
\\toprule
 & $\\rho = 0.6$ & $\\rho = 0.95$ \\\\
\\midrule
Pooled OLS & %s & %s \\\\
Fixed effects & %s & %s \\\\
Anderson--Hsiao (one instrument) & %s & %s \\\\
Arellano--Bond (all lags, one-step) & %s & %s \\\\
\\bottomrule
\\end{tabular}
\\end{center}
", s6[1], s95[1], s6[2], s95[2], s6[3], s95[3], s6[4], s95[4]))
```

- **At $\rho = 0.6$ the fix works.** Both IV estimators sit inside the bracket, near the truth; Arellano--Bond is the tighter.
- **At $\rho = 0.95$ it does not.** Anderson--Hsiao is scattered across the number line; Arellano--Bond is pulled far down with an enormous spread --- the signature of weak instruments.

## System GMM: the idea, and its price

Blundell and Bond's repair: keep the differenced equation, and **add the levels equation back**, instrumented the other way round:
$$
Y_{it} = \rho\,Y_{i,t-1} + u_i + \varepsilon_{it}, \qquad \text{instrument } Y_{i,t-1} \text{ with } \Delta Y_{i,t-1}
$$

- **Why it helps.** A level cannot predict a random walk's next step --- but **a firm that just rose is high**. The first-stage coefficient of $Y_{i,t-1}$ on $\Delta Y_{i,t-1}$ is exactly $\tfrac12$ for every $\rho$. It never dies.
- **What it costs.** The levels error contains $u_i$, so you need $\mathbb{E}[\Delta Y_{i,t-1}\,u_i] = 0$: **a firm's changes must say nothing about its permanent level.** True in the two-firm picture, *because both firms start at their own long-run levels*: **mean stationarity**.
- **When to doubt it.** Firms observed from IPO start away from their targets and converge; a panel that starts after a crisis has everyone off target together. Then rising *does* reveal a high-$u_i$ firm, and the extra instruments are invalid.

## Every estimator, on one line

```{r one-line}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 2.1
#| out-width: 92%
#| fig-align: center
labs <- c("OLS", "FE", "AH", "AB", "System")
ttl  <- c(expression(rho == 0.6), expression(rho == 0.95), expression(rho == 0.95 * ", firms start off target"))
tru  <- c(0.6, 0.95, 0.95); xl <- c(0, 1.3)
par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(2.4, 3.4, 1.4, 0.4), mgp = c(1.4, 0.4, 0), cex = 0.85)
for (k in 1:3) {
  s <- sims[[k]]; q <- apply(s, 1, quantile, c(.1, .5, .9)); y <- 5:1
  plot(NA, xlim = xl, ylim = c(0.5, 5.5), yaxt = "n", xlab = expression(hat(rho)), ylab = "", main = ttl[k], cex.main = 1)
  axis(2, at = y, labels = labs, las = 1, tick = FALSE)
  rect(q[2, "fe"], 0, q[2, "ols"], 6, col = "grey90", border = NA)
  abline(v = tru[k], lty = 2, lwd = 1.5)
  lo <- pmax(q[1, ], xl[1]); hi <- pmin(q[3, ], xl[2])
  segments(lo, y, hi, y, lwd = 2)
  out_l <- q[1, ] < xl[1]; out_h <- q[3, ] > xl[2]
  if (any(out_l)) arrows(xl[1] + 0.08, y[out_l], xl[1], y[out_l], length = 0.05, lwd = 2)
  if (any(out_h)) arrows(xl[2] - 0.08, y[out_h], xl[2], y[out_h], length = 0.05, lwd = 2)
  points(q[2, ], y, pch = 19, cex = 1.1)
  box()
}
```

\footnotesize Shaded: the bracket. Dashed: the truth. Dots: medians; bars: 10th--90th percentiles over 200 draws. \normalsize

- **$\rho = 0.6$:** every IV estimator lands inside the bracket, near the truth.
- **$\rho = 0.95$:** the difference estimators collapse (weak instruments); system GMM holds ($`r f2(med$b["sys"])`$).
- **Firms start at the average level, not their own:** Arellano--Bond recovers ($`r f2(med$c["ab"])`$); system GMM lands at $`r f2(med$c["sys"])`$, **above OLS** --- the bracket catches it. **Each estimator fails exactly when its own assumption does.**

## Long panels: a different route

When $T$ is large the problem is milder, and a different tool is available.

- **Bias-corrected FE.** The fixed-effects bias is $O(1/T)$ **with a known formula**: estimate FE, subtract the bias at $\hat\rho$, iterate (Kiviet 1995; Bruno 2005 for unbalanced panels; Stata's `xtlsdvc`). No instruments, no weak-instrument problem --- but the other regressors must be **strictly exogenous**, which finance controls rarely are.
- **Long differences** --- $Y_{it} - Y_{i,t-k}$ --- keep the instruments strong even for persistent series (Hahn, Hausman and Kuersteiner 2007).
- **Horse race.** On finance-like panels --- short, persistent, unbalanced --- Flannery and Hankins (2013) find bias-corrected FE and system GMM generally reliable, and difference GMM frequently not.
- **Rule of thumb.** $T \le 10$, $\rho$ moderate: Arellano--Bond with the diagnostics. $\rho$ near one: system GMM, with mean stationarity defended. $T \ge 20$ and exogenous controls: bias-corrected FE.

# 5. In Practice

## A case study: how fast do firms adjust leverage?

The partial-adjustment model is our equation with $Y$ = leverage and $1-\rho$ the **speed of adjustment**.

\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabular}{llcc}
\toprule
Paper & Estimator & $\hat\rho$ & speed $1-\hat\rho$ \\
\midrule
Fama and French (2002) & pooled (Fama--MacBeth) & $\approx 0.85$ & $\approx 7$--$18\%$ a year \\
Flannery and Rangan (2006) & fixed effects (IV for lagged leverage) & $\approx 0.66$ & $\approx 34\%$ \\
Lemmon, Roberts and Zender (2008) & system GMM & $\approx 0.75$ & $\approx 25\%$ \\
Huang and Ritter (2009) & long differencing & $\approx 0.80$ & $\approx 17$--$23\%$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

- **The ordering is the bracket.** Fixed effects reports the *fastest* adjustment, pooled estimation the *slowest*; the IV-type estimates sit between.
- Whether firms rebalance toward targets or just drift **turned on the bias this lecture is about**: a half-life of $1.7$ years and one of $5$ are different theories of the firm.
- Caveat: the papers differ in samples, periods and leverage definitions. The ordering is suggestive, not a controlled horse race.

sd_draw <- rbind(ols = c("0.918", "0.999", "1.083"),
                 fe  = c("0.334", "0.592", "0.840"),
                 ah  = c("0.596", "1.077", "1.004"),

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="68%"}

```stata
clear all
set seed 20260202
local rho = 0.6                      // then 0.95
set obs 500
gen firm = _n
gen u = rnormal()                    // firm effect
* start each firm at its own long-run level
gen y = u/(1-`rho') + rnormal(0, 1/sqrt(1-`rho'^2))
expand 8
bysort firm: gen year = _n
xtset firm year
by firm: replace y = `rho'*y[_n-1] + u + rnormal() if _n > 1

reg   y L.y, vce(cluster firm)                    // up
xtreg y L.y, fe vce(cluster firm)                 // down
ivregress 2sls D.y (LD.y = L2.y), vce(cluster firm)
xtabond  y, lags(1) maxldep(3) twostep vce(robust)
xtdpdsys y, lags(1) maxldep(3) twostep vce(robust)
```

## The code, on real data

```stata
* 1. The bracket first -- and keep both numbers
reg   y L.y x i.year, cluster(firm)
xtreg y L.y x i.year, fe cluster(firm)

* 2. Difference GMM (Arellano-Bond): two-step, Windmeijer SEs, lags 2-4 of y
xtabond y x i.year, lags(1) maxldep(3) twostep vce(robust)
estat abond                       // AR(1) expected; AR(2) must be absent

* 3. Same, with collapsed instruments and the Hansen test (Roodman's xtabond2)
ssc install xtabond2
xtabond2 y L.y x i.year, gmm(y, lag(2 4) collapse) iv(x i.year) noleveleq twostep robust
*    x predetermined rather than exogenous? replace iv(x ...) with gmm(x, lag(1 3) collapse)

* 4. System GMM -- only after you have defended mean stationarity
xtdpdsys y x i.year, lags(1) maxldep(3) twostep vce(robust)

* 5. Long T, exogenous x: bias-corrected fixed effects
ssc install xtlsdvc
xtlsdvc y x, initial(ab) bias(3) vcov(50)
```

- In R: `plm::pgmm()` with `transformation = "d"` (difference) or `"ld"` (system); `pdynmc` for the Roodman-style options.

## A reporting checklist

\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabular}{R{5.2cm}R{7.4cm}}
\toprule
Report & Because \\
\midrule
$\hat\rho_{\text{OLS}}$ and $\hat\rho_{\text{FE}}$ & the bracket; your estimate must sit inside it \\
AR(1) and AR(2) tests & AR(2) tests the identifying assumption \\
Hansen $J$, the instrument count, lag depth, collapsed or not & $J$ is informative only when the count is small relative to $N$ \\
one-step and two-step (Windmeijer) side by side & disagreement signals weakness \\
difference vs.\ system GMM, with mean stationarity defended & they rest on different assumptions \\
what $D$ is assumed to be (exogenous / predetermined / endogenous) & it determines which lags of $D$ are valid instruments \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

- Each row is a place where the estimator can silently fail, and a number the reader needs to decide whether it did.

## Conclusion

1. **A lagged $Y$ is endogenous by construction**, not by omission. You can read the problem off the model.
2. **One rule does every calculation**: later shocks are unrelated to earlier $Y$; the same-date shock enters with coefficient one. Check dates.
3. **OLS is biased up and fixed effects down.** Run both first --- **the bracket is the goalposts.**
4. **The fix is a longer lag of the same variable.** $Y_{i,t-2}$ is one date too early to be contaminated. Arellano--Bond uses all such lags; cap and collapse them.
5. **The fix fails when the series is persistent or firm effects are large** --- the normal case in finance. Then: system GMM if firms sit at their own long-run levels, or bias-corrected FE if $T$ allows.

\vspace{0.3em}

- The question to carry out: **which way is this estimator wrong?** If you can say that, you can say where the truth lies.
- **Next:** difference-in-differences --- when the switching has a *date*.

# Backup

## Bracketing $\delta$: lagged $Y$ or fixed effects?

When you are unsure **which model** is right --- lagged $Y$, or fixed effects --- and what you care about is $\delta$, the two estimates bracket it too.

\begin{center}\small
\begin{tabular}{lll}
\toprule
If the truth is & and you estimate & then $\hat\delta$ is \\
\midrule
the lagged model & fixed effects      & too \textbf{high} \\
the fixed effects model & the lagged model & too \textbf{low} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

- As written, for $\delta > 0$; if $\delta < 0$ the directions swap. (Angrist and Pischke 2009, §§5.3--5.4.)
- Run both and report the bracket rather than picking the specification you prefer.
- **If the bracket excludes every sensible value, stop.** The model is wrong in some other way.
